welcome: ccdash is a dashboard for viewing Claude Code and Codex usage, costs, and workflows together.
We’ll start with how to read the opening screen, then follow user activity, model calls, and tool usage.
The values on screen are example data for explaining the features.
architecture: In this example setup, a local Collector gathers telemetry and stores it in ClickHouse through an authenticated ingestion path.
The browser displays results queried by the Express API.
Browser sign-in and device ingestion credentials are separate.
The two Express boxes in the diagram represent logical roles within the same application.
language: Choose from five languages at the bottom of the sidebar.
On mobile, open the menu to make your selection.
Your selection persists across visits, and your open work and query period stay as they are.
The guide also opens in the same language.
window: Before comparing, align the client, backend, and supported user and model filters.
The date range lets you enter start and end times to the second, as well as dates.
Time fields use your browser’s time zone; the date picker uses the UTC calendar.
Share links preserve the same interval, but check the server’s aggregation interval and ingestion delay separately.
overview: In Overview, start with costs, observed tokens, sessions, and users.
The trend below is a starting point for finding busy periods.
Read the cost basis and partial-total indicators beside the totals.
Unavailable data is not zero, and the presence of values alone does not mean collection is complete.
executive: Use Executive for a quick view of overall usage and cost composition.
After aligning the period and collection scope, compare the client and model mix.
Channels in Claude details are distinctions inferred from sessions.
They do not represent experiment groups or individual performance.
trends: In Trends, compare with the previous period to see when tokens, costs, and activity changed.
When you spot a spike, narrow to a shorter interval and open Users or Cost with the same filters to investigate.
users: Select a user row in Users to see that user’s totals, usage trend, and activity periods.
Finding users with high costs is a starting point for investigating work, not evaluating performance.
Distinguish the masked display from actual API access permissions.
range: Drag across the usage and cost charts in user details to narrow to the time range you want.
User details stay open, while the top 20 work items update to that period.
Select a bucket by clicking a point.
Check the model and workflow labels, then open the work you want to inspect.
trace: In Trace details, review total tokens, cost, and call count as you follow the timeline.
Even when Explore types match, separate agents appear in separate lanes.
Distinguish model calls, tool executions, and periods spent waiting for user approval.
Use the cumulative cost chart and lanes together to find when and which agent accumulated costs.
call: Select a call bar to see the model, duration, input and output tokens, and cache tokens.
The cost source indicates whether it was reported by the client or calculated as an estimate.
Sources can differ even within the same work item.
TTFT and attempt details appear only when collected.
Do not interpret blank values as zero or as meaning there were no retries.
context: Select a point in the context graph to return to that call.
The model calls table helps highlight related calls.
In the session environment, check observed MCP connection status, loaded plugins, and the context of the first call.
Information that is not collected, such as the token size of each tool definition, cannot be determined from this screen alone.
cost: In Cost, compare how costs are distributed across models, users, and backends.
First check the basis for reported and estimated costs.
Claude reported values, AWS list-price estimates, and calculation diagnostics have different meanings.
None of these values is an invoice or guarantees the actual bill.
Zero-cost items appear in a collapsed list; items with unknown costs are marked unestimated.
economics: Productivity’s cost equation links users, sessions, turns, requests, tokens, and unit prices to explain total cost.
The driver breakdown shows which factors increased or decreased the amount from the previous period.
Even when unit prices fall, total costs can rise if usage increases by more.
These are observed measures of activity and efficiency, not causal evidence of investment impact or employee productivity assessments.
unit: Compare cost per user, session, or amount of code only when the required denominator and collection scope are available.
The dashed line in the unit-cost trend is a visual guide connecting unknown intervals for readability.
Those intervals are not treated as measurements or calculated as zero.
usage: In Usage, compare the mix of input, output, and cache tokens alongside tool usage.
Check whether cache and reasoning tokens are subsets of total usage to avoid double counting.
Also look at changes in request counts and context size.
tools: In the tools table in Claude details, compare executions, errors, and latency to find recurring failures.
The permission decision table is different from tool execution results.
Approval does not mean execution succeeded; distinguish automatic approval from requiring user approval each time.
If you find a problem period or user, return to the work Trace to inspect the actual calls.
mcp: In MCP, see which servers and connectors were used and compare their calls and success rates.
Connection status and actual usage are different kinds of information.
If you see failures, also check that work’s tool executions and session environment.
skills: In Skills, compare which skills were used and how they were invoked.
Distinguish direct calls, automatic activation, and continuation from another skill.
Costs attributed to a skill are not separate charges to add again to total costs.
Read this as telemetry for finding related sessions and work.
plugins: The plugin list shows which extensions were loaded into a session.
Being loaded does not by itself mean a feature was executed.
Check the session environment along with model, agent, and command configuration to investigate why the same work differs across environments.
reliability: In Reliability, review errors, response times, versions, and cost diagnostics.
Look at distributions and periods where problems cluster, not just a single average.
When usage falls, first distinguish a real drop in activity from ingestion delays or missing data.
analytics: Analytics provides a closer look at models and diagnostic signals.
Question-based analysis is also available when permissions and model settings are in place.
For question-based analysis, check the executed query, the result period, and the cost basis.
This screen shows example diagnostic data.
Do not add Codex metrics or diagnostic Traces back into completion-log usage or cost.
collector: Once the server is ready, register a device from the Collector installation menu, then run the authenticated dashboard’s installation command in that device’s terminal.
The device token is displayed once; store it as instructed, and do not expose its value in a command or screen share.
In the device list, check registration details and revoke ingestion credentials when needed.
installation: In Installation status, check the database connection, per-client receipt status, and schema check results.
Available menus and check scope depend on your permissions.
If you find a problem, follow the guide’s installation and operations procedures, then check the same query interval again.
finish: Start by aligning the period, then select users where costs or usage differ.
Follow the work, calls, and tools to find the next place to investigate.
The guide includes every menu, practical procedures, and screens you can zoom in on.
Continue exploring in whichever language you prefer.
